Schedule

Regulations for the International Controlled Transactions Schedule (ICTS) were laid before the House of Commons on 4 November 2026.

HMRC has published guidance on the regulations in the International Manual at INTM917300 and INTM917400.

HMRC aims to publish the ICTS notice on 26 November 2026 and detailed guidance on the ICTS notice by 31 December 2026.

The ICTS is a new annual reporting requirement for businesses within scope of UK transfer pricing or permanent establishment rules.

Businesses within scope will need to provide HMRC with specified information about cross-border related party transactions for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027.

Agents and advisers should use the guidance to help identify clients who may be affected and help them understand the requirements.

Share the guidance with relevant networks and clients.

Important changes to Automatic Exchange of Information — action required

This article covers 2 key deadlines you need to be aware of:

the Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI) will temporarily close from 15 December 2026 until early January 2027

Electronic Money Institutions must register for the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) by 31 January 2027

These changes may affect financial institutions you represent.

AEOI service closing on 15 December 2026 — what you need to do

HMRC is introducing a new digital service for Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) reporting.

To prepare for this, the current AEOI service will close at 3pm on 15 December 2026. The first phase of the new service opens in early January 2027.

While the service is unavailable, you and your clients will not be able to:

register

submit CRS or FATCA reports

correct or amend CRS or FATCA reports

You must complete any outstanding CRS and FATCA submissions, corrections and amendments before 3pm on 15 December 2026.

You should also:

check that your contact details are up to date

tell relevant colleagues and clients that the service is closing

We will provide an update when the first phase of the new service is live. Existing AEOI service users will not need to register again.

If you have clients who are Electronic Money Institutions

As previously shared in Agent Updates, changes to CRS 2.0 implemented from 1 January 2026 mean that Electronic Money Institutions have new obligations.

Read more in previous Agent Update editions:

December Agent Update

May Agent Update

If your clients hold Specified Electronic Money Products or Central Bank Digital Currencies on behalf of customers, they are considered a Depository Institution for CRS purposes.

Clients who are within scope will have registration, due diligence, and reporting obligations to HMRC. They must register for CRS by 31 January 2027, even if they do not have any reportable accounts.

Clients who have already registered do not need to do it again.

Help test the registration service

We are looking for Electronic Money Institution volunteers to test the new CRS registration service before it opens to everyone. Volunteers will receive dedicated support with registration. Their feedback will help us improve the service for other users.

To take part, Electronic Money Institutions should email nimco.huseen@digital.hmrc.gov.uk with ‘CRS Beta Testing’ in the subject line.

Share this information with relevant clients.

Key dates

15 December 2026 at 3pm: the current service closes

early January 2027: the first phase of the new service opens

31 January 2027: deadline for Electronic Money Institutions to register for CRS

Reporting functionality will be introduced later in 2027. We will publish guidance in advance to explain what reporting financial institutions need to do.

Where to find help

Read more on the Automatic Exchange of Information agreements collection page for guidance on CRS registration and reporting.

For technical guidance on CRS, including due diligence requirements and an overview of the new penalty regime, read the International Exchange of Information Manual.

If you still have questions, email aeoi.enquiries@hmrc.gov.uk.

Updated guidance on mandatory reporting of benefits in kind

We are updating our guidance to prepare for mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind. This will help agents, stakeholders, employers and third-party benefit providers get ready for the changes with detailed information and examples to help them prepare well ahead of mandatory reporting of benefits in kind in real time from 6 April 2027.

From 6 April 2027, company cars, car fuel, vans, van fuel, and medical benefits will no longer be included in the employees’ tax codes.

Employers will need to:

report these benefits through payroll

deduct tax due directly from employees pay in real time

pay the associated Class 1A National Insurance contributions

Globally mobile employees

Agents are encouraged to inform their clients that employers will have the option to exclude eligible globally mobile employees from mandatory payrolling through a new exception cases service.

Employers must complete the new online exception cases form available from 5 November 2026 to notify HMRC.

Employers should continue to use existing year-end reporting arrangements for these employees through forms P11D and P11D(b). Our updated guidance explains the definition and process for globally mobile employees.

Voluntarily payrolling other benefits

From 5 November 2026, employers can register to voluntarily payroll non-mandated benefits in kind (BiKs) for the 2027 to 2028 tax year using the online Payrolling Benefits and Expenses service.

Employers must register on or before 5 April 2027 to use this service. Employers already registered for voluntary payrolling will automatically be carried over to the 2027 to 2028 tax year.

HMRC agent services

HMRC bulletin for Corporation Tax agents and advisers

Remind clients to submit their Company Tax returns

Every year, more than 100,000 companies fail to file their Company Tax return within 12 months of its statutory filing date. In May 2026, more than 20,000 companies had returns that were over a year late.

Companies must submit their Company Tax return by their statutory filing deadline, even if they have no Corporation Tax to pay.

HMRC may charge penalties for late returns. If a company does not file a return, HMRC may use the information it holds to issue a determination. This is an estimate of the Corporation Tax the company owes.

The company must still submit its return and pay any tax, interest, and penalties due.

Tax agents and advisers play an important role in helping companies meet their Corporation Tax obligations. However, the company and its directors remain legally responsible for meeting these obligations, even when an agent acts on their behalf.

If your clients have outstanding returns to file

Remind your clients to file any outstanding returns. This will help them to avoid being charged further late filing penalties, determinations, and compliance checks.

If a company has stopped trading, its directors should inform HMRC as soon as possible and file any outstanding returns. They may also wish to apply to have the company dissolved through Companies House, where appropriate.

Read more information on:

Corporation Tax

Accounting periods for Corporation Tax

Paying Corporation Tax

Filing a Company Tax Return

‘Be Ready’ campaign

The government’s new ‘Be Ready’ campaign helps people to take simple, practical steps to prepare for everyday risks and emergencies such as floods, fires and power cuts.

The principle behind it is simple: being prepared means frontline services can focus on those who need the most help during an emergency.

The Cabinet Office developed the campaign with input from the public.

Trusted partners supporting the campaign include:

the British Red Cross

National Emergencies Trust

local councils

emergency services

local resilience forums

Other countries have been running similar campaigns for many years, so this brings us into line with many of our neighbours.

Read and share the details of this important campaign with friends and family.

Changes to the ‘Where’s my reply’ tool

Customers can use the ‘Where’s my reply’ tool to check when they can expect to receive a response from HMRC to a query or request they made.

Agents can also use the tool to check how long HMRC is likely to take to:

process an application made on behalf of a client

process a request to change their agent details

Based on your feedback, we are improving the tool so you will now receive a more accurate response.

We are introducing the changes in stages, and we have focused on the 5 highest volume work areas:

SA appeals and penalties

Marriage Allowance

P87 — employment expense repayments

R40 claims for a refund of Income Tax deducted from certain types of income, particularly from savings and investment

registering for Self Assessment

Your feedback showed that the tool did not always give an accurate response time. In many cases, you received a reply sooner than the date shown. The changes mean most users will get a more realistic, expected reply date based on the normal timeframe for their request.

HMRC has achieved its target of clearing 80% of correspondence within 15 working days so far this year. If your request is taking longer, the tool will continue to show the longest expected waiting time, which is what happens now.

Once we have reviewed the first phase, we will be working on enhancing the tool to include all work areas.

Agents to use the Agent Dedicated Line for employer-related queries

We are encouraging all tax agents with employer-related queries to contact the Agent Dedicated Line, rather than the Employer Helpline.

This change is part of an ongoing trial. By bringing employer-related queries into the Agent Dedicated Line we will help provide a more consistent service for agents. This will help to make sure queries are handled by advisers with specialist knowledge of agents’ needs and the issues they encounter.

The trial will also give us greater insight to inform future improvements for agents.

The Employer Helpline will remain available for queries from individuals.

Top tips for Self Assessment

Every year we see common mistakes and avoidable issues in Self Assessment that can delay processing or create extra work for agents and their clients. These practical tips highlight some of the most frequent problems and explain what you can do to get things right.

Registering and reactivating for Self Assessment

Submitting a tax return for a client who has not registered for Self Assessment, or reactivated their Self Assessment record after a period of not filing, can lead to delays in processing, incorrect tax calculations and incorrect repayments.

Here’s how to get it right:

check if your client needs to complete a tax return

register new clients using the online CWF1 form for self-employed clients or the SA1 form for others

reactivate an existing Self Assessment record if your client already has a Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR) and needs to start filing again — use the online CWF1 or SA1 form to do this

Tax

Help your clients make sure new employees are paid correctly from day one

Getting new starter details right first time helps your clients avoid extra administration, reduces payroll errors and reassures employees that they are being paid correctly from day one.

Your clients can help make the process smoother by following 3 simple steps:

Ask new employees for key personal information before they start, including their full name, date of birth and National Insurance number.

Use a P45 or the online starter checklist to set up PAYE correctly and send accurate information to HMRC.

Encourage new employees to download the HMRC app. They can use it to check their tax code, National Insurance number, annual tax summary and employment history.

Share these steps with your clients to help them avoid common new starter errors.

Guidelines for Compliance — GfC22 — help to prevent payroll errors and PAYE RTI disputed charges

HMRC has recently published new Guidelines for Compliance: Help to prevent payroll errors and PAYE RTI disputed charges.

These guidelines are for employers and those who process payroll on behalf of employers. They may also be useful for tax agents and professional bodies advising clients or members about their payroll obligations.

A Real Time Information (RTI) disputed charge occurs when the amount an employer believes they owe in PAYE differs from the amount shown on HMRC’s systems. This can result in either a credit or debit on the employers account.

The guidelines provide practical support to help employers avoid payroll submission errors, reducing the likelihood of disputed charges arising.

The guidelines help by:

providing background information on RTI disputed charges

highlighting the most common errors

explaining how to avoid these errors

explaining what to do if a mistake is made

Read more information on the Guidelines for Compliance collection.

Guidelines for Compliance — GfC21 — help with VAT on cryptoassets

HMRC published new Guidelines for Compliance to help with VAT on cryptoassets on 15 October 2026.

The guidelines are for UK and overseas businesses involved in cryptoasset transactions where UK VAT may apply. This includes:

businesses that sell or exchange cryptoassets

artists and creators who supply cryptoassets directly to customers

operators of digital platforms or marketplaces through which other people make supplies

The guidelines may also be useful to agents and advisers acting for these businesses.

They bring together existing VAT principles and explain how they apply to cryptoasset activities. They do not introduce new VAT rules.

The guidelines explain:

what HMRC means by cryptoassets for the purposes of the guidelines

when a business may need to register for VAT

how the VAT treatment depends on what is supplied and how it is used, rather than the name or description of a token

what customer and transaction information businesses should collect and retain

how to establish whether a customer is a business or private consumer and where the customer belongs

how the place of supply and electronically supplied services rules may apply

when a digital platform or marketplace may be responsible for accounting for VAT

what to do if a business identifies a previous VAT error or is unsure about the correct treatment

Agents should consider the guidelines when advising clients that sell or exchange cryptoassets or facilitate supplies of them.

Agents should help clients check that they have:

correctly identified the underlying supply

met any VAT registration obligations

collected enough evidence of the customer’s status and location

established who is responsible for accounting for VAT when a platform is involved

Following the guidelines will help businesses reduce the risk of errors, VAT adjustments and penalties.

Changes to Climate Change Levy

HMRC is modernising the administration of the Climate Change Levy (CCL). As part of these changes, existing customers will receive a new CCL reference number.
